title: Is that so?
hook: Hakuin is wrongly blamed for a child, raises him, is later cleared, and says only "is that so?" (Zen story, Japan)
carry: the child in front of you

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was hōge, letting go: Tanzan set the woman down at the river, and Ekido carried her all day. Your line was I set her down at the river.
screen: `I SET HER DOWN AT THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: Somebody gets you wrong. A rumor at work. A friend who believes the worst. A comment online from someone who's never met you. And the speech starts writing itself: let me explain, you don't understand, how dare you. Now meet Hakuin, a Zen teacher and painter of Japan, whom Rinzai Zen tradition honors as one of its great masters. One morning, the story goes, angry parents bang on his door, holding a newborn baby, and accuse him of something he never did.
screen: `SOMEONE GOT YOU WRONG.` → `LET ME EXPLAIN!` → `HAKUIN AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: A young woman in the village is pregnant, and won't say who the father is. Her parents press her, and finally she names Hakuin, the monk up the road. When the baby is born, the furious parents carry it to his door. This is yours, they say. Take it. And Hakuin says only: is that so? He takes the baby. His good name is gone. People who bowed to him in the road now look away. He asks the neighbors for milk, and cares for the child. He doesn't argue or explain. A year later, the young mother can't bear it anymore. She tells her parents the truth: the father is a young man who works at the fish market. The parents run back up the road, full of shame, apologizing, begging to take the child home. Hakuin hands the baby back. And he says: is that so? Nobody can say for certain this happened; it's a story told about Hakuin, not a record. But look at what those three words do. They aren't agreement: he never says yes, it's mine. And they aren't a fight. They just receive the news. Blame arrives, and he meets it the same way he meets praise. And in between, the thing that needed doing, caring for a baby, got done. It's easy to spend everything on the story about you. Hakuin spent his on the child in front of him. That's the hard part, and the free part.
screen: `THIS IS YOURS. TAKE IT.` · `HIS GOOD NAME IS GONE.` · `THE TRUTH COMES OUT.` · `SAME WORDS FOR BLAME AND PRAISE.` · then, large: `IS THAT SO?`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something someone said about you, fair or unfair, praise or blame, and notice what your body does with it: the rush to defend, or the glow of being liked. Say inside, slowly, not yes, not no, just: is that so. Then turn your attention to one thing in front of you that needs care.
Hakuin. A Zen teacher who met blame and apology with the same three words, while caring for the child in front of him.
Your line: the child in front of you. Not the story about you. Day forty-five, done.

screen: `DAY 45 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE MOON CAN'T BE STOLEN.`

howItsDone: Zen teachers tell the story of Hakuin's "is that so?" to describe equanimity, meeting praise and blame alike, and Rinzai Zen tradition remembers Hakuin as a teacher who renewed it.

original.note: Japanese, sō desu ka: is that so? an everyday phrase. The story doesn't record Hakuin's exact Japanese words.

notes: Hakuin Ekaku (1686–1769), reviver of Rinzai Zen and painter: confirm the brief description.
The story is told in Zen Flesh, Zen Bones (not public domain); paraphrased. Historicity not claimed; the script says so. The 'fish market' detail follows the common telling.
Japanese そうですか (sō desu ka) is offered as the everyday phrase; the tale's exact Japanese wording is unknown, and the note says so. Some retellings use そうか (sō ka).
The review segment uses capital 'I' in the carry line, as in the index.
